newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish Solidarity in national protest on shipyard.
newsitem.headline: Polish Solidarity in national protest on shipyard.

text.p: Poland's Solidarity union launched nationwide protests on Wednesday to demand rescue for the collapsing Gdansk shipyard and reacted with fury when riot police ousted workers occupying Warsaw government ministries.

"A horrible provocation" was how the rightist trade union's leader Marian Krzaklewski described to reporters a decision by the ex-communist-led government to send police to expel scores of workers from the Economy, Treasury and Finance ministries. @
Solidarity began the national action on Wednesday, after a receiver this month announced plans to wind up the Baltic coast yard where Solidarity arose in defiance of communism in 1980.

While about 2,000 demonstrating shipyard workers in Gdansk bricked up the door to offices of the ruling ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), which Solidarity accuses of allowing the yard's collapse, scores of workers in Warsaw moved in to occupy the three ministries.

After issuing an ultimatum police cleared the ministries, leading to scuffles at the Treasury in which, union officials told PAP news agency, one worker was beaten unconscious and others were injured. Witnesses said police were also injured.

"Once more the Red authorities are using force against a peaceful demonstration," protest leader Kazimierz Grajcarek told a news conference as the police action began, adding that union reinforcements were converging on the capital.

Krzaklewski told reporters Solidarity's national committee would meet on Thursday in Warsaw to decide a response. He said the union could in theory call a general strike if force was used against it, although it would try other options first.
He alleged that police had intercepted two buses bringing workers to the capital and had beaten some miners. Police spokesmen could not immediately be reached for comment.
Solidarity's protest campaign aims to force a rescue of the shipyard and help for other workers facing job losses in industries such as coal-mining in the southern Silesia region.

It is also stirring emotions in the approach to parliamentary elections due around September this year, by reviving the divisions in society left over from the struggle that led to the toppling of communist rule in 1989.

The union has formed rightist parties into a powerful Solidarity Election Action (AWS), to take on the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) which has shared power in coalition with a Peasant party since 1993.
Finance Minister Marek Belka, who blames bad management for the yard's plight, told a news conference there was a chance some of its jobs and plant could still be saved.
He was apparently referring to proposals Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz is to put to parliament on Thursday.
Gdansk radio reported this plan might involve the more successful Szczecin shipyard building ships in Gdansk for the Polska Zegluga Morska (PZM) merchant marine company.
The government blames bad management for the Gdansk yard's plight and has refused to pressure banks to finance the building there of five ships for a German shipowner, saying the contract was flawed.
The yard's receiver announced earlier this month he would dismiss its last 3,800 employees, and sell the assets piecemeal, after banks refused $100 million in credit to the shipyard.
